title: Earthquakes: When the Ground Shakes
summary: How moving plates in the Earth's crust get stuck and suddenly slip, how scientists measure earthquakes, why the Red Sea is growing wider, and how people stay safe.
poll: Getting ready for an earthquake is more useful than trying to guess when one will happen.

versions.title: When the Ground Shakes
versions.text:
Can the ground shake? Yes! That is a quake.

The top of the Earth is a hard skin. It is the crust. The crust is cut in big parts. Each part is a plate. The plates move. They move as slow as your nails grow.

Two plates push. Their edges get stuck. Then they slip all at once! This lets out lots of energy. The energy shakes the ground.

The quake starts deep down. The spot right on top is the epicenter. The shake is worst there.

Most quakes are small. We do not feel them. Big ones can break homes. A quake in the sea can make a huge wave.

A tool can feel each quake. It gives the quake a number. A big number means a strong quake.

Our land is on a plate, too. It moves away from Africa. So the Red Sea gets a bit wider each year.

No one knows when a quake will come. So learn to be safe. Drop down. Get under a desk. Hold on.

versions.title: The Day the Ground Shook
versions.text:
Most of the time, the ground is still. But at times it shakes hard. This is called a quake.

The top of the Earth is a hard, rocky layer. It is called the crust. The crust is cut into huge parts called plates. The plates move all the time. They move as slow as your nails grow.

Where two plates meet, their edges rub. Then the edges get stuck. The push grows and grows. At last the rock slips all at once. This sends out a burst of energy. The energy runs through the ground and makes it shake.

A quake starts deep down. The spot on top, right above it, is the epicenter. The shake is worst there.

Most quakes are small, and we do not feel them. Big ones can knock down homes. A quake under the sea can push up a huge wave.

Each quake is felt by a tool. The tool gives it a number. A big number means a strong quake.

Saudi Arabia sits on its own plate. It moves slowly away from Africa. That is why the Red Sea grows a bit wider each year. Experts here watch the ground with care.

No one can tell when a quake will come. So we learn to stay safe. Drop to the floor. Get under a desk. Hold on till the shaking stops.

The outer layer of the Earth is called the crust. It is made of hard rock. It is broken into huge pieces known as tectonic plates. These plates are always moving, but very slowly. They creep along at about the same speed that your fingernails grow.

Where two plates meet, their edges press and grind against each other. Sometimes the rough edges get stuck. The plates keep pushing, so stress builds up in the rocks. It is like a spring being squeezed tight. Then the rocks slip all at once. This lets out a huge burst of energy. The energy moves through the ground in waves and makes it shake.

An earthquake begins deep underground. The place on the surface directly above that point is called the epicenter, and the shaking is usually strongest there.

Most earthquakes are so small that people never notice them. But large ones can knock down buildings and break roads. A quake under the ocean can lift the water. Then it makes a giant wave called a tsunami.

Scientists record earthquakes with a machine called a seismometer. They describe the size of each quake with a number called its magnitude. A bigger magnitude means a much stronger earthquake.

Saudi Arabia sits on its own plate. It is slowly moving away from Africa. Because of this, the Red Sea becomes a tiny bit wider every year. Scientists in the Kingdom watch the ground carefully with their own instruments.

Nobody can tell just when an earthquake will happen, so people get ready instead. Engineers plan strong buildings that can bend without breaking. Students practice what to do: drop to the floor, take cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on until the shaking stops.

Most of the time, the ground beneath our feet seems perfectly solid and dependable. Occasionally, however, it begins to tremble without any warning: dishes rattle in the cupboard, lamps swing from the ceiling, and the floor appears to roll like a wave. This sudden shaking is called an earthquake, and it is one of the most powerful natural events on our planet.

The outer layer of the Earth, known as the crust, consists of hard rock that is fractured into enormous sections called plates. These plates fit together like the pieces of a gigantic puzzle, and they are constantly moving, although extremely slowly. They creep along at roughly the same speed that human fingernails grow.

Where two plates meet, their edges press and grind against each other. Because the rock surfaces are rough, friction often prevents them from sliding smoothly, so the edges become locked together. The plates continue pushing, and pressure gradually accumulates in the rocks, much like a spring being squeezed tighter and tighter. Eventually the rocks slip suddenly along a crack called a fault, releasing a tremendous burst of energy that travels outward in seismic waves and causes the ground to shake.

An earthquake begins deep underground. The point on the surface directly above that starting place is called the epicenter, and the shaking is usually most violent near it, growing weaker with distance.

The vast majority of earthquakes are so small that people never notice them. Powerful ones, however, can collapse buildings and split roads apart. When an earthquake occurs beneath the ocean floor, it can lift an enormous volume of water and generate a destructive wave called a tsunami.

Scientists record seismic waves with sensitive instruments called seismometers. They describe the size of each earthquake with a number called its magnitude, and every step up in magnitude represents a dramatically more powerful event.

Saudi Arabia occupies its own plate, which is gradually separating from Africa. As a consequence, the Red Sea becomes slightly wider every year. Scientists in the Kingdom monitor the ground continuously, relying on a network of stations distributed across the country.

Because nobody can predict exactly when an earthquake will strike, communities prepare instead. Engineers design reinforced buildings that can flex without collapsing, and students practice the correct response: drop to the floor, take cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on until the shaking stops.

The Red Sea is the most dangerous place on Earth.
Tsunamis cause more damage than any other natural event.
Earthquakes result from moving plates releasing stored energy, so people measure them and prepare.
questions.why: The article explains the cause of earthquakes, how scientists measure them, and why communities prepare.

wrong.A: Most quakes are small, but strong ones are felt by everyone and cause damage.
wrong.B: The Red Sea is an example of plate movement, not called the most dangerous place.
wrong.C: The article does not compare tsunamis to all other events.

questions.stem: Read: "friction frequently prevents them from sliding smoothly." What does friction mean?
options: A sudden flash of light from the rocks
The force that resists rubbing surfaces
A liquid that makes rocks slippery
The heat inside the Earth's center
questions.why: Friction is what stops the rough rock surfaces from sliding, so the edges lock together.

wrong.C: Friction makes sliding harder, not easier.
wrong.D: The sentence is about surfaces rubbing, not the Earth's center.

questions.stem: Why do the edges of two plates become locked together?
options: Their rough surfaces create friction
Water freezes between them
Scientists hold them in place
The plates stop moving completely
questions.why: The article says the rock surfaces are rough, so friction keeps them from sliding smoothly.

wrong.C: Scientists measure plates; they cannot hold them.
wrong.D: The plates keep pushing, which is why pressure builds.

questions.stem: According to the article, where do the rocks slip when an earthquake begins?
options: At the top of a mountain
In the middle of the ocean waves
Along a fracture called a fault
Inside a seismometer
questions.why: The article says the rocks slip abruptly along a fracture called a fault.

wrong.A: Earthquakes begin deep underground, not on mountaintops.
wrong.B: Waves are in the water, not where rocks slip.
wrong.D: A seismometer records waves; rocks do not slip inside it.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer from the final paragraph?
options: Strong buildings can stop earthquakes from happening at all.
Because the timing is unknown, being prepared is the best protection.
Students are the only people who need to get ready for earthquakes.
Scientists will soon be able to predict every earthquake exactly.
questions.why: Since nobody can predict when an earthquake will strike, the article stresses preparation by engineers and students.

wrong.A: Buildings reduce damage; they do not stop earthquakes.
wrong.C: Engineers and whole communities prepare too.
wrong.D: The article says nobody can predict precisely when one will strike.

questions.stem: Why does the author include information about Saudi Arabia and the Red Sea?
options: To argue that people should move away from the coast
To compare the Red Sea with other oceans
To explain how ships cross the Red Sea
To show that plate movement affects the region where readers live
questions.why: The example connects plate movement to the Kingdom, making the science feel close to home.

wrong.A: The article does not tell anyone to move.

questions.stem: One earthquake has a magnitude of 7, and another has a magnitude of 5. Which conclusion is supported by the article?
options: The magnitude 7 earthquake was much more powerful.
The two earthquakes released the same energy.
The magnitude 5 earthquake was more dangerous.
Magnitude tells only how long the shaking lasted.
questions.why: Every step up in magnitude represents a dramatically more powerful event, so 7 is far stronger than 5.

wrong.B: Different magnitudes mean different amounts of energy.
wrong.C: A lower magnitude means a weaker earthquake.
wrong.D: Magnitude describes the size of the earthquake, not its length.

questions.stem: How do scientists in the Kingdom keep track of earthquakes?
options: By asking people to report shaking
By watching the Red Sea from boats
Through a network of stations
By measuring how fast fingernails grow
questions.why: The article says they monitor the ground with a network of stations distributed throughout the country.

wrong.A: Reports from people are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Fingernails are only used to compare the speed of plates.

HIGH.prompt: Is it more useful to try to predict earthquakes or to prepare for them? Support your opinion with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence connects to my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think it is more useful to prepare for earthquakes than to try to predict them. The article says nobody can predict exactly when an earthquake will happen, so instead engineers design reinforced buildings that can bend without breaking along a fault. Scientists also monitor the ground with instruments to understand seismic activity, but this does not tell them the exact moment friction between the plates will finally let go. Since we cannot know the timing, practicing safety steps ahead of time saves more lives than waiting for a prediction.
